"We should do the survey online," Rajni said, for the third time. "It's faster."
"And we'll only reach people who are already online," Mehak said. "Our topic is street vendors, Rajni."
Rajni felt her jaw set. She was the group leader. She could simply decide.
She put her pen down. "Okay. Tell me why you think vendors won't answer online."
"Most of the ones near college don't use email. Some don't read English."
"Fair. But face-to-face takes three weekends."
Anil, who had been quiet, said, "Why don't we test it? Ten online, ten in person, this Saturday. See which gets real answers."
Rajni hesitated. "Fine. If in-person is better, we go with it."
On Saturday the online forms got two replies. The in-person ones got ten, with stories.
Rajni sighed at the results sheet. "In person it is. I was wrong."
Mehak grinned. "You were fast. I was careful. We'll need both."

qa.q: What was the group's topic?
qa.a: Street vendors.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when her jaw set?
qa.a: Frustrated, and tempted to use her position as group leader to override Mehak.

qa.q: How did the group settle the disagreement?
qa.a: By hearing each other's reasons, testing both methods with ten surveys each on Saturday, and accepting the result.

qa.q: How did Mehak respond to Rajni admitting she was wrong?
qa.a: Graciously, grinning and saying the group would need both Rajni's speed and her own care.

grounding: Shows a strong disagreement over a project approach, settled by listening, testing the ideas with data and accepting the result.

In our final-year app project, Damini wanted a simple list view. I wanted a map, because maps look impressive. We argued for two meetings. When the group voted for her list, I went silent for a week, did my part badly, and told myself they'd regret it.
On user-testing day we put both versions in front of twelve students from the hostel. Nine of them finished the task faster with the list. Two got lost in my map. One said, "The map is pretty, but where's the button?"
I stood there feeling embarrassed, and then oddly relieved. The data had decided, not Damini.
I apologised to the group for sulking. I rebuilt the list screen properly, and Damini let me add a small map on the details page, where it actually helped.
Next time I disagree, I want to say "let's test it" in the first meeting, not after a week of silence.
— Yash

qa.q: How many students tested the two versions?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: How did Yash feel on user-testing day?
qa.a: Embarrassed at first, then oddly relieved that the data had decided rather than Damini.

qa.q: What does Yash want to do differently next time?
qa.a: Suggest testing the ideas in the first meeting instead of sulking for a week.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt during Yash's silent week?
qa.a: Frustrated and uneasy, carrying the project while a teammate sulked.

grounding: Illustrates a clash over a design idea, the pitfall of sulking after the group's decision, and learning to test ideas with data.

For their NSS water survey in Kolar district, Hemant had taken charge of everything: which wells to visit, who asked what, even who carried the clipboard. At the gram panchayat office he answered every question himself while Farida and two others stood behind him.
On the walk back past the paddy fields, Farida's stomach churned. Staying quiet was easier. But she had grown up in a village like this one and knew the women came to the handpump at 6 a.m., not at noon, when Hemant had scheduled the visits.
That evening she said, "Hemant, the noon visits are missing most of the women. In my aunt's village it's the same; they fetch water at dawn. Can we switch?"
He frowned. "I've already planned it."
"I know. Can we write down who leads which village? I'll take the dawn visits in two villages." She had already drawn up the table.
The others nodded. Hemant looked at the paper, then agreed, a little stiffly. At dawn on Friday, Farida's clipboard filled up within an hour.

qa.a: At noon.

qa.a: Uneasy, with her stomach churning, and tempted to stay quiet because it was easier.

When our team split the documentary project, I handed the editing to Gopika. Then I watched every second. I messaged her four times a day: "Did you trim the intro?" "Use the other music." "Can you send me the file?" On Wednesday she replied, "Do you want to just do it yourself?" and went offline.
That stung, because she was right. I didn't trust anyone with my idea.
I called her that night and apologised. We agreed on two checkpoints instead: a rough cut on Friday and a final cut on Monday, and I would comment only then. When the rough cut came, I wrote three notes, starting with what I loved, the way she opened on the fisherwoman's hands. Then two changes.
The final version was better than mine would have been. I told her so.
— Vasudha

Lab supervisor's note, robotics club, 3 March
This week I watched Manoj, the team captain, hand the motor-control code to Hrithik, a second-year. Last year Manoj rewrote other people's code at midnight without telling them, and the team nearly fell apart.
This time was different. On Monday Manoj said, "It's yours. Can we check on Wednesday and Friday? I'll only look then." On Wednesday Hrithik's code made the robot spin in circles. Manoj laughed, then said, "Your structure is clean. The turning speed is too high. Want to try halving it?" He didn't touch the keyboard.
On Friday the robot ran the course in forty seconds. Hrithik looked proud; Manoj looked like someone trying hard not to interfere, and mostly succeeding.
I told Manoj afterwards that this is what leadership looks like. I have asked him to share the checkpoint idea at next week's club meeting.

qa.q: How long did the robot take to run the course on Friday?
qa.a: Forty seconds.

qa.q: What did Manoj seem to feel on Friday?
qa.a: Proud of Hrithik and a little restless, trying hard not to interfere.

qa.q: How did Manoj give feedback kindly on Wednesday?
qa.a: He laughed, praised the clean structure first, named one problem, the turning speed, and suggested a fix without touching the keyboard.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel about being trusted with the code?
qa.a: Proud and capable, especially when the robot finished the course.

grounding: Illustrates trusting a teammate with a part, agreeing on checkpoints and giving kind feedback instead of micromanaging.

Salma closed her laptop halfway. "It's not ready."
It was ready. It just looked thin next to Ritu's section, which had diagrams, three case studies and a professor's comment saying "excellent".
Ritu raised an eyebrow. "We submit in two days."
Salma sighed and opened the laptop. "Okay. Honestly? I didn't want you to see it because yours is so good. I felt stupid."

"Four. Want me to show you how I found the case studies? It's one database."

They sat for an hour. Salma found two case studies of her own and rewrote her opening.
"Better?" she asked.
"Better. And now it sounds like you, not me."

When our economics group got a C on the policy paper, the group chat went quiet for an hour. Then Farida wrote, "The data section was the problem. Pooja, you were in charge of that."
My face burned. My first instinct was to agree with everything, apologise for the whole paper and disappear. My second was to point out that Farida's conclusion had contradicted the data anyway.
I did neither. First I reread the professor's comments carefully. Two of the five were about my data section: outdated figures and no source for one table. That part was mine. The other three were about the argument and the conclusion.
So I wrote: "I've read the comments. The outdated figures and the missing source are on me, and I'm sorry. Three comments are about the argument, which we all wrote. For the next paper, can we check each other's sections a week before?"
Farida replied after a while: "Fair. I'll go through the data with you next time."
— Pooja

qa.a: By reading the comments first, owning the two about the data section, noting that the other three were shared, and proposing peer checks a week before.

The group's bridge model failed at half the target load today. Afterwards Pankaj told the others, loudly, "Ganga did the joints. That's why." Ganga went pale and said, "It's all my fault. I ruined it for everyone." She was close to tears.

Vaibhav, beta, you keep checking your phone. Someone stopped replying? Let me, your Binita pishi, tell you a story from before phones.
In 1985 I was twenty, in Shillong, writing every week to a boy called Arun whom I'd met at a cousin's wedding. For six months he wrote back, long letters with pressed leaves inside. Then nothing. I wrote three more letters. Then a fourth, angry. Then I walked to the post office every day for a month, asking the postman if something had got lost.
I decided I'd been too boring. Too forward. Too something.
Years later a friend told me Arun had simply got engaged and hadn't known how to tell me. So he told me nothing. It had nothing to do with my letters.
I wish I had stopped at the first unanswered letter and kept my own peace. His silence was about his courage, not my worth. So, beta, put the phone down and come and eat. Your pishi has made luchi.

qa.q: What did Arun put inside his letters?
qa.a: Pressed leaves.

qa.q: How did Binita feel about herself when the letters stopped?
qa.a: That she had been too boring or too forward; she felt small and blamed herself.

qa.q: What does Binita wish she had done?
qa.a: Stopped at the first unanswered letter and kept her own peace, instead of writing more and asking the postman every day.

qa.q: Why had Arun stopped writing?
qa.a: He had got engaged and didn't know how to tell her, so he said nothing.

grounding: Illustrates being ghosted, the urge to chase and self-blame, and learning that the other person's silence was about them, not one's worth.

Three dates in, Tejas knew. Ishita was kind and funny, and he didn't feel anything more than that. Her message had been sitting on his phone since Tuesday: "Movie this weekend? 🙂"
He had opened it four times on the metro between Andheri and Ghatkopar and closed it each time. It would be so easy not to reply. People did it all the time. She'd get the hint.
Then he remembered last year, when someone he liked had vanished on him, and he'd spent a week wondering what he had done wrong.
He got off at his station, sat on a bench and typed: "Hi Ishita, I've really enjoyed our evenings, and I want to be honest: I don't think this will be more than friendship for me. Sorry to say it by text, but I didn't want to leave you guessing. Have a good weekend."
He read it three times and sent it. It felt awful for about ten minutes. Then lighter.
Her reply came an hour later: "Thanks for telling me. Honestly, I appreciate it."

Anand and Tanuja had walked to the same school in their village in Wardha district for ten years. When she moved to Nagpur for nursing college, they spoke every Sunday. Then, in March, nothing. No calls, no replies, for four months.
At the tea stall near the bus stand, Anand's friend Mukesh said, "She's a city girl now. Post something on her photo, let her feel it."
Anand was tempted. He was hurt. But he remembered Tanuja at eight, sharing her tiffin when his mother was ill.
That night he sent one message: "Tanuja, I miss our Sunday calls. I hope you're okay. No need to reply if you're busy. I'm here whenever." Then he stopped checking.
In August a reply came: "Sorry, Anand. Papa was in hospital for months. I couldn't talk to anyone. Your message helped."
He called her that evening. They talked for five minutes. It was enough.

After Pankaj stopped replying in October, I did something I'm not proud of: I replayed our last conversation about two hundred times. Was it the joke about his job? The way I said "see you soon" too eagerly? I scrolled up so often I knew his messages by heart.
One night my friend Shirin found me doing it at 1 a.m. in the hostel common room. She sat down and said, "You've told me this story five times this week. Has it changed?"
It hadn't. That was the loop. Hearing it named helped.
She said, "Write him the goodbye he didn't give you. Don't send it." So I did, in my notebook: what I enjoyed, what hurt, and that I was done waiting. It took twenty minutes. At the end I felt tired but lighter.
I still think of him sometimes. But now when the replay starts, I notice it, and I text Shirin instead of scrolling.
— Ujjwal

qa.q: How many times did Ujjwal replay the last conversation?
qa.a: About two hundred times.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling while replaying the conversation?
qa.a: Hurt and anxious, blaming the joke about the job and the too-eager "see you soon".

qa.q: What helped Ujjwal step out of the loop?
qa.a: Shirin naming the loop, writing an unsent goodbye in a notebook, and texting Shirin instead of scrolling when the replay starts.

qa.q: How does Shirin see Ujjwal's retelling?

grounding: Shows replaying what went wrong after being ghosted, noticing the loop, talking to a friend and giving oneself closure.

Counsellor's note, student wellness centre, 7 December
Irawati came in today, her third visit. Her close friend Hafsa stopped replying two months ago, after a disagreement over a group trip. Irawati said she has been lying awake "rewriting every message" and has decided the friendship ended because she is "too much".
I asked her to list, on paper, the evidence for "too much". She found one argument and two late replies. Then I asked what she would tell a friend in her place. She laughed a little: "That they're not the only one in the story."
We talked about noticing the loop: when she catches herself rereading the chat, she will write the thought down, then text her cousin or go for a walk. She also plans to write herself a closing note to Hafsa that she will not send.
Her shoulders looked less tight when she left. We meet again next week.

qa.a: Two months ago.

qa.q: What had Irawati decided about why the friendship ended, and how was it affecting her?

qa.q: What plan did Irawati make with the counsellor?
qa.a: Notice the loop, write the thought down and then text her cousin or walk, and write an unsent closing note to Hafsa.

qa.q: What does Irawati's answer about "not the only one in the story" suggest about Hafsa's part?
qa.a: That Hafsa also played a part, so the silence isn't only Irawati's fault.

grounding: Illustrates rumination and self-blame after being ghosted by a friend, and noticing the loop and giving oneself closure with support.
